title: A Interior for the Silence
premise: Dominic Quintana, a professional translator who has spent thirty years erasing the village dialect of their childhood, returns to the family house days before its demolition and finds a cache of undelivered letters hidden behind a wardrobe—letters written by their grandmother in that dying language, addressed to family members who never received them. As Dominic translates each letter, they uncover how the family's silence was manufactured: a bargain made during hard years in which one member was cast out so the rest could survive, and every relative since has paid rent on that silence with small betrayals. The demolition date becomes a deadline for truth; at a final gathering in the emptying house, Dominic reads the last letter aloud, forcing the question the whole family arranged itself around—who did we sacrifice, and what did it buy us? The novel ends not with reconciliation but with something harder: the family choosing to carry the story openly, as the house comes down and Dominic finally speaks the old language aloud without translating it away.
about_author: Lena Pemberton is a former court interpreter who grew up between two languages and one long family silence. She writes literary fiction about inheritance, translation, and the things families agree not to say.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. In the city, Dominic works flawlessly between languages while deflecting all personal questions with a practiced smile, until a call from a cousin: the childhood house is scheduled for demolition in three weeks, and someone has to come sort it. Emotional beat: the cost of invisibility made visible.

chapters.title: What the Wardrobe Kept
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Arriving at the half-gutted house, Dominic finds a bundle of letters in dialect wedged behind a wardrobe panel—all in their grandmother's hand, none ever delivered. The first letter names someone Dominic has never heard mentioned. Emotional beat: curiosity cracking open dread.

chapters.title: A Language of Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Alternating present-day and memory from Dominic's POV. Translating the first letter, Dominic realizes how much of the dialect they've lost, substituting standard words where the old ones fail. Flashbacks show a grandmother teaching a child words she forbade elsewhere. Emotional beat: grief for a tongue still technically alive.

chapters.title: The Uncle Who Wasn't Discussed
chapters.summary: Cousin Marisol's POV. Marisol arrives to help clear the house and reacts strangely to the name in the letters: Tomás, her father, sent away in 1974 and never spoken of again. She warns Dominic to stop reading. Emotional beat: loyalty versus the itch of the forbidden.

chapters.title: Rent Paid in Small Betrayals
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Letter by letter, the mechanism emerges: the family survived a ruinous debt by making Tomás the scapegoat for an accident, and each member's prosperity was built on his exile. Dominic recognizes their own silence-keeping as inherited labor. Emotional beat: complicity arriving like cold water.

chapters.title: Marisol's Version
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Confronted privately, Marisol admits her father wrote to the family for years and every letter went unanswered; she found one as a teenager and burned it out of fear. She begs Dominic to let the demolition bury everything. Emotional beat: shame weaponized into pleading.

chapters.title: The Question Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The penultimate letter reveals the grandmother knew everything and chose silence to keep the family intact, addressing her final words to whoever found them: 'Ask them what we bought.' With the demolition two days away, Dominic must decide whether to force the gathering. Emotional beat: resolve hardening against comfort.

chapters.title: Everyone Arrives Angry
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, anchored in the aunt Beatriz's POV. Dominic summons the scattered family to the emptied house under a false pretext; when the letters appear on the kitchen table, old alliances fracture—denial, blame, and Beatriz's furious defense of the original bargain as survival, not cruelty. Emotional beat: the family's architecture collapsing on schedule.

chapters.title: Read It Aloud
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV, climax. In the bare front room, Dominic reads Tomás's last undelivered letter—in the old dialect, stumbling but unflinching—describing a life lived in the shadow of a lie he never understood. Beatriz breaks; Marisol confesses the burned letter; the room goes quiet enough to hear the question land. Emotional beat: truth as demolition from within.

chapters.title: An Interior for the Silence
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV, resolution. The house comes down; the family does not heal cleanly but agrees to find Tomás or his children and tell them everything, keeping the letters as evidence rather than secret. Dominic, changed, begins translating nothing—for once just speaking the language, aloud, to whoever will listen. Emotional beat: belonging rebuilt on shared weight instead of shared silence.
